source: Morris, Croker, Zimmerman, Gill, Romine (2013) Gaming science: the gamification of scientific thinking
finding: Review says scientific thinking does not develop routinely. It needs schooling and cultural tools. Evidence interpretation is biased by prior beliefs even in educated people.
numbers: No new data. Cites Kuhn and Franklin 2006 p.974 for 'does not routinely develop'.
limits: Secondary review; no effect sizes. Frames science as dual search over hypotheses and experiments (Klahr and Dunbar 1988).
agent_relevance: Controlled testing is a taught skill, not a default. A scaffold must impose it in code, not hope the model shows it.

source: Kuhn and Franklin (2006) The development of scientific thinking skills (as cited in Morris et al. 2013)
finding: Cited claim: scientific thinking is highly educationally mediated, and interpreting evidence is subject to prior-belief bias.
numbers: Not read directly; no numbers seen.
limits: Known only through a citing paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a guardrail that revisions come from real output, not the model's prior belief (G2).

source: Montes, van Dijk, Puche, van Geert (2017) Trajectories of scientific reasoning: microgenetic study of children's inquiry
finding: Four 5-year-olds solved three computer multivariable tasks on moving objects. Inquiry did not grow in a straight line. It had advances, relapses, exploratory states and transitions.
numbers: N=4 children (multiple case study), 3 tasks, short and long time scales.
limits: Tiny sample; descriptive only. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Even after one good test, the next may regress. Check each test for control again; do not assume the habit is stable.

source: Chen and Klahr (1999) All other things being equal: acquisition and transfer of the control of variables strategy, Child Development 70(5)
finding: Founding study. As cited by later papers: young elementary children can learn the control-of-variables strategy (CVS) by direct instruction, but do not use it spontaneously until about grade 4.
numbers: Exact figures not retrieved this session (publisher page blocked, 403). Left out rather than recalled from memory.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: S4 'one change per test' is teachable by explicit instruction. A prompt rule should state it plainly, not rely on discovery.

source: Klahr and Nigam (2004) direct instruction vs discovery learning; Vollmeyer and Burns (1996); Chinn and Malhotra (2002) (all as cited in Kaiser, Mayer, Malai 2018)
finding: Cited: direct instruction teaches CVS better than discovery. Rival: Vollmeyer and Burns say undirected exploration gives richer learning of how a system works. Chinn and Malhotra: once students understand CVS they adopt it almost routinely.
numbers: Not read directly; no numbers seen.
limits: Authors call it 'some controversy'.
agent_relevance: Instruct the rule, then allow exploration. Rule teaching and free exploration may serve different goals.

source: Kaiser, Mayer, Malai (2018) Self-generation in the context of inquiry-based learning, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Students (grades 6-7) who generated CVS through inquiry did not beat students who read it. Reading did better on a pooled test, and the first-test gap vanished within a week.
numbers: 2 (self-generation vs reading) x 3 (immediate, 1 week, 4-6 weeks) ANOVA: condition F(1,107)=4.32, p=.040, partial eta2=.039, reading better. First test: reading M=4.06 (SD 1.31) vs generation M=3.41 (SD 1.62), t(125.58)=2.58, p=.011, d=0.44. Two-point ANOVA interaction F(1,131)=3.72, p=.056, partial eta2=.028 (not significant).
limits: Real school setting; teachers may have kept teaching between tests.
agent_relevance: Self-generating the rule gives no lasting edge over being told it. Tell the agent the rule.

source: Schlatter, Molenaar, Lazonder (2020) Individual differences in children's development of scientific reasoning through inquiry-based instruction, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Fifth-graders improved on a written scientific reasoning test over a 5-week inquiry unit, but unevenly. Experimenting (CVS) gained. Hypothesis-evidence coordination and drawing conclusions did not gain significantly.
numbers: N=138 (ages 8-12, 55% boys, mostly 10). Progress came between lessons 1 and 3, not 3 and 5. Reading and math predicted CVS gain scores: 0.253 and 0.202 (both p<.001; estimates as printed).
limits: No control group in the passages read. CVS pre-test did not relate to reading or math, post-test did.
agent_relevance: Coordinating theory with evidence is harder to improve than controlling variables. Expect the agent to need explicit help on the evidence-to-theory step.

source: Schlatter, Molenaar, Lazonder (2020) (sub-group result)
finding: Authors expected either high pre-test CVS with little gain, or low pre-test with large gain. A small cluster of children made a large improvement; most did not.
numbers: Cluster size not stated in the text read.
limits: Post hoc sub-group.
agent_relevance: Averages hide a split: some learners get the rule at once. Test the agent per item, not only on average.

source: Sobel, Koksal, Osterhaus, Bachhuber, Moeller (2026) Longitudinal relations between representational and advanced theory of mind and scientific reasoning, Developmental Science
finding: Theory of mind at age 4 predicted scientific reasoning at 5.5, directly and through advanced theory of mind at 7.5. This held after controlling executive function and language, which also related to reasoning.
numbers: Longitudinal at 4, 5.5 and 7.5 years. Executive function was a significant individual predictor in one model.
limits: Correlational. Sample size not captured. Measures differ across ages.
agent_relevance: Controlled testing may rest on thinking about what one's own evidence can show. Motivates a step where the agent states what a result could and could not tell it.

source: Osterhaus and Koerber (2023); Koerber and Osterhaus (2020) (as cited in Sobel et al. 2026)
finding: Cited: 6-year-olds (not 5-year-olds) who passed second-order false belief used CVS better. Separately, content knowledge at age 5 predicted reasoning at 6, but not the reverse.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Citation only. Direction of effects disputed across studies.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge in context may matter as much as the rule.

source: Developmental trajectories in diagnostic reasoning: understanding data are confounded develops independently of choosing the control of variables (2022), Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Preschoolers showed each skill partly, but the skills were unrelated. Recognising confounded evidence did not predict choosing a controlled test.
numbers: N=57, ages 3-6. About 70% recognised a controlled two-variable test at least once, above chance overall. Over two-thirds did so with three variables. Just under half justified the choice (two variables), over one third (three variables). On confounded evidence just over half noticed ambiguity at least once; about a quarter said confounded data cannot support a unique conclusion. No significant correlation between task types.
limits: Small N; accuracy only slightly above chance in places; two-variable CVS choices correlated negatively with age. Authors' reading (metacognitive link absent) is one of several.
agent_relevance: Choosing a good test and judging a bad test are separate skills. The agent needs a rule for designing tests (S4) and a separate check that flags confounded results.

source: Chen and Klahr (1999) definition of confounded (as cited in the 2022 preschool paper)
finding: Cited: a comparison is confounded when the variable of interest and one or more others vary together, so no single effect can be separated.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Defines a failure a code check can detect: more than one factor differs between two runs.

source: Seifert, Harrington, Michal, Shah (2022) Causal theory error in college students' understanding of science studies, Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications
finding: Advanced college students often accept a causal claim from correlational evidence. A short example-based lesson on alternative causes reduced the error, and the gain held one week.
numbers: 240 enrolled, 97 (40%) completed all three sessions. Pre-lesson: 66% found a correlational study convincing; 63% endorsed a decision based on it. Over 75% of both accepting and rejecting groups chose a third-variable diagram. Post-test ratings differed from pre-test (LSD p=.043 and p=.027).
limits: Voluntary sample, 60% dropout, no separate control group, written answers.
agent_relevance: Theory-evidence coordination fails even in trained people. 'List alternative causes before accepting a claim' helped. Fits G3.

source: Mueller and Coon (2013); Sumner et al. (2014); Xiong et al. (as cited in Seifert et al. 2022)
finding: Cited: intro psychology students made 28% error on correlational findings, falling to 7% by term end. Causal claims reached over 80% of associated media stories. 63% of people drew causal inferences from non-experimental data as often as from experiments.
numbers: Figures as quoted in the Seifert introduction.
limits: Second-hand; not opened.
agent_relevance: Human baseline error for theory-evidence coordination is high, so matching humans is a low bar.

source: Molnar and Csapo (2018) The efficacy and development of students' problem-solving strategies during compulsory schooling: logfile analyses, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: In a large school study, students who used vary-one-thing-at-a-time (VOTAT) knowingly solved best, then VOTAT users without awareness, then non-VOTAT users. Using a good strategy did not always give good results.
numbers: n=4,371 students, grades 3-12 (ages 9-18), MicroDYN problems of varying complexity, latent class analysis of logfiles. Order: conscious VOTAT > non-conscious VOTAT > non-VOTAT.
limits: Awareness inferred from action sequences, not asked. Success depended on complexity and age.
agent_relevance: One change per test is not enough alone. The agent must also use the result of each test.

source: Tschirgi (1980); Funke (2014); Schoppek and Fischer (2017) (VOTAT work as cited in Molnar and Csapo 2018)
finding: Cited: VOTAT is the most effective strategy for finding input-output links in a small complex system. After rounds of practice people used it more, and used it better. Systems that change on their own also need a vary-none-at-a-time run.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Pair S4 with a no-change control run when the environment can change by itself.

source: Wang, Jansen, Cote, Ammanabrolu (2022) ScienceWorld: Is your agent smarter than a 5th grader?
finding: Text agents do far worse at doing elementary experiments than at answering science questions. Models can state a known material's conductivity but struggle to run an experiment on an unknown one.
numbers: Best agents reached normalised average score 0.17 across tasks. A 1.5M-parameter agent trained interactively for 100k steps beat an 11B model trained on static science QA. 5 seeds.
limits: 2022 agents (GPT-2, T5-based), not current frontier models.
agent_relevance: Knowing the rule is not doing the rule. Run the controlled test in code or a tool, not only describe it.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Baseline GPT-4o agents did poorly at end-to-end discovery. Expert human scientists did far better.
numbers: 120 tasks, 8 topics, 3 difficulty levels, 5 seeds. Best completion: ReAct 38% easy, 18% challenge. Best knowledge discovery: Hypothesizer 34% easy, 8% challenge. Humans (up to 11 per task, 16 tasks): 66% completion, 55% knowledge, 11 of 16 tasks above 60%.
limits: Only GPT-4o tested; GPT-4o grader.
agent_relevance: The human-model gap is largest on hard tasks that need many variables.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld (NeurIPS 2024) (unit tests)
finding: On small component tasks (such as measuring with instruments) agents reach moderate scores. They fail when parts must be chained into a full discovery.
numbers: 10 unit tasks, max 100 steps: completion in the 60%+ range per the authors.
limits: Exact per-agent figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: Chain failure, not component failure, is the problem. The state machine should supply the chaining.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld (NeurIPS 2024) (variable-measuring tasks)
finding: On proteomics clustering tasks that need more variables measured, ReAct scored zero completion on both the 2-variable and 5-variable versions, and Plan+Execute scored zero on 5 variables.
numbers: Normal 'Measure 2 variables': ReAct completion 0.00. Challenge 'Measure 5 variables': ReAct 0.00, Plan+Execute 0.00 (5 seeds).
limits: One task family; zero may reflect setup as much as variable control.
agent_relevance: More variables, worse results. Agents may need an explicit one-factor-at-a-time plan as variable count grows.

source: Gandhi, Li, et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Language-model agents struggle at both choosing informative experiments and building models from data. Larger models beat smaller; closed beat open.
numbers: 10 environments. 32B models beat 7B. Prior information often did not help; models sometimes did better with 0 experiments than after some. GPT-4o had the lowest expected-information-gain regret with strong prediction. Qwen-32B had higher regret despite good prediction.
limits: Workshop pre-print (NeurIPS 2025 SEA). EIG is measured under the simulator's own model.
agent_relevance: Good prediction and good experiment choice come apart. Judge tests by information gained, not answer accuracy alone.

source: Gandhi, Li, et al. (2025) BoxingGym: benchmarking automated experimental design and model discovery (explanations)
finding: A written explanation from an experimenting agent helped a novice agent less than running the experiments directly.
numbers: Novice agents given explanations scored worse than experimenters; help varied by environment (useful for animal tasks, weak for moral-judgement tasks).
limits: Effect sizes not extracted from figures.
agent_relevance: Handing results over as prose loses information. Pass raw output between steps.

source: Huang, Vora, Liang, Leskovec (2024) MLAgentBench: evaluating language agents on machine learning experimentation
finding: A Claude 3 Opus agent was best of those tested on ML experiments, but success varied widely by task.
numbers: 13 tasks. Average success 37.5% (improve baseline by 10%, 8 runs). Range 100% (house-price) to 0% (BabyLM).
limits: Success means a 10% gain, not sound method. Newest tasks failed most.
agent_relevance: Agents run experiment loops well on familiar tasks and fail on novel ones. Do not assume good test design transfers.

source: Chen, Chen, Ning, et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench (ICLR 2025)
finding: Language agents solve a minority of real data-driven science tasks. Extra inference compute helped.
numbers: 102 tasks from 44 papers, 4 disciplines, 9 experts. Best agent 32.4% alone, 34.3% with expert knowledge. Without executing code, Claude-3.5-Sonnet solved 16.7% (20.6% with knowledge). OpenAI o1 variants up to 42.2%.
limits: Data analysis tasks, not controlled-experiment design. 3 attempts per task.
agent_relevance: Running code to see output about doubles success. Supports G2: revise from real output.

source: Evidence gap note (Angle B)
finding: Not found this session: any LLM study that directly tests control-of-variables or confounded-evidence judgement with human-style items. Web search budget, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API were all rate limited.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Absence reflects tool limits, not a finding. Schwichow et al. 2016 meta-analysis, Kuhn microgenetic studies, Klahr and Nigam 2004 and Chen and Klahr 1999 were not opened.
agent_relevance: Re-run with working search before the schema relies on a CVS-specific claim.
